text:
If I have to prove that I’m the man, being the man has already become an act, and I have to defend it every time I hesitate, cry, need help, or get something wrong.

I don’t actually walk around thinking I’m some super-masculine guy. I cry, I need help, I get things wrong. Bee once called me her “wife.” I don’t recommend that as a polarity exercise, by the way.

When a woman appreciates that masculine side of me, it tends to come out by itself.

The same is true for a woman: she should not have to perform softness, helplessness, or cuteness every minute to prove she is feminine. Surrender means so much more when she could take control but prefers not to at that moment. When a strong woman surrenders, she is choosing to, which is sexy.

Women can get pulled in two directions here. She may worry that I don’t find her beautiful enough, or that she’s too emotional, too difficult, not logical enough, or too needy. Then she can over-correct into needing nobody, and receiving care or letting a man lead starts to feel like weakness.

Toft says that after fifty years he still tells his wife she’s beautiful, including finding new kinds of beauty as she ages. Anami talks a lot about women learning to receive. Letting a man help, lead, or give her pleasure doesn’t make a strong woman helpless, and a man who receives care is still a grown man. Sometimes that’s as ordinary as a woman who knows perfectly well how to drive asking me to drive because she likes how it feels when I do; she’s choosing the experience. I might ask, “Honey, how do you see this intuitively?” because I actually want her use her power, and she might ask me to help think through the practical side because she wants that from me.

That’s called invitational: Would you rather go to a party where you were invited or a war you got drafted into?

When a woman doesn’t know how to gently invite a man to lead, she may manufacture a crisis until the man is forced to take charge to get the same outward result.

Unfortunately, I’ve seen a lot of the latter.
reader: A man and a woman in a relationship, working out how each can be strong and still lean on the other.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
